Bourd Originals Portfolio

E. Bourd's #2 problems (his own or joint with Claude) composed during our sessions that could go to magazines as originals. Built from knowledge/problems.json: every entry re-solved and passed through tools/blog.py check on 18 Oct 2026 (sound, legal, no fatal flaw, no identical position in Problemesis or his PDB). The anticipation check is identical-position only: search yacpdb/PDB before sending. Left out: schemes, sketches, post-key positions, bench demonstrations he called schemes, illegal or promoted-force positions, and versions superseded by a later one. 'fen' overrides the stored FEN where a verified trim exists. Tiers: 1 send first (most content for its flaws), 2 sendable, 3 thin or a clear flaw, single = one phase without tries or changes (E. Bourd, 18 Oct 2026: not for publication unless very complicated or pretty), gate = fails the gate now (needs a fix or his override), public = already shown on the blog. 'tries' names thematic tries the notes describe only in words.

Explanation

Task: two different units defend on the same square, mates changed. Rd6-d4 and Se2-d4 self-block d4 (a diagram flight). Try 1.e6? (2.Qe5#): Rd4 2.Bxg6#, Sd4 2.Rg4#, Rxe6 2.Qd5#, but 1...Bg7!. Sc4 is pinned by Ra4 (so Sxd2 is impossible and 1...Kd4 2.Rxc4#). bPg6 stops Qf5 (try dual), bPh4 stops Sg3 (key dual): each alone looks removable, together they are not.

Key

Explanation

Black Qf6 and Bd4 both capture the knight e5. Each capture opens a White battery for the OTHER mate: Bxe5 vacates d4 and opens Rc4-f4 (front piece Se4), Qxe5 self-blocks and the Bf5/Rf8 battery fires. Set: Qxe5 2.Bg6#, Bxe5 2.Sg5#. Try 1.Qxh1? (2.Qf3#) Qxe5 2.Bh3#, Bxe5 2.Qf1# but 1...g2!. Key 1.Qg2! (2.Qf3#) Qxe5 2.Bh3#, Bxe5 2.Sxg3#: Bxe5 answered three ways across three phases, Qxe5 two ways; the mate chosen by where the White queen stands (Qh3 guards g4 so any Bf5 departure mates, Qg2 is blocked by the g3 pawn so only Bh3 covers g4). Dual avoidance unified: each sibling mate gives no check because the other battery line is still closed. Flaws: 22 units and 10 pawns; d5 (answers Kxf5) and e6 (stops Qe6) only stop cooks; Ka8 idle; the non-thematic tries carry six-fold bishop duals after Qxe5. Flight-giving key (f5). Verified sound by the Python solver.

Doubled Dombrovskis on captures of two different white units, with white correction tries. Heavy.

Key ['Bc5'] · E. Bourd

2b1KB2/3p4/4N1N1/1P1kPBp1/1P4R1/1P1pp3/pbrr4/q1R5

Set
1...Rc4 2.bxc4#
Try
1.Bg7? (2.Se7#) but 1...Bxe5!
Try
1.Bd6? (2.Se7#) but 1...Bxe5!

Try

Key
1.Bc5! (2.Sc7#) 1...Rxc5 2.Rxc5#, 1...Bxe5 2.Se7#, 1...dxe6 2.Be4#
Explanation

Doubled Dombrovskis on two captures of two different white units. The e6 knight is the only guard of d4 and the e5 pawn the only guard of d6. Try 1.Ke7? (2.Be4#) is refuted by dxe6! (the guard of d4 goes, Be4+ Kd4); tries 1.Bg7?, 1.Bd6? and 1.Re4? (2.Se7#) are refuted by Bxe5! (the guard of d6 goes, Se7+ Kd6). Key 1.Bc5! covers d4 and d6 with one quiet move and threatens Sc7#; now dxe6 (which captures the threatening knight) allows 2.Be4# and Bxe5 (which guards c7 through d6) allows 2.Se7#; third variation Rxc5 2.Rxc5#. The two paradox defences carry the same weight: each removes a unique guard of one square beside the king and the key piece takes over both squares, which is the balance he asked for. Two of the tries are moves of the key bishop, a white-correction flavour. Flaws: 22 units with a seven-unit black cluster (Qa1, Bb2, Rc2, Rd2, Pa2, Pd3, Pe3) that stops cooks and provides the Rxc5 variation; three tries with one refutation; passive white king.

bourd-pawn-steps-changed

gate pass1 tries · 2 changed

Pawn single and double step as self-blocks, changed between 1.Be6? e4! and 1.Ke4! (zugzwang, king key).

Key ['Ke4'] · Evgeni Bourd

2B5/2p1N3/3k4/3NpK2/8/3pQ3/3P4/8

Set
1...c5 2.Qxe5#/Qh6#
Try
1.Be6? (zugzwang) 1...c6 2.Sc8#, 1...c5 2.Qxe5#, but 1...e4!
Key
1.Ke4! (zugzwang) 1...c6 2.Sf5#, 1...c5 2.Qh6#
Explanation

1.Ke4! (zugzwang) c6 2.Sf5#, c5 2.Qh6#; try 1.Be6? c6 2.Sc8#, c5 2.Qxe5# but 1...e4!. Both steps are self-blocks, each on a square guarded by a different white piece: c6 was the knight e7's square (so the knight is released), c5 the queen's (e3-c5, so the queen is released). That gives the split of the mates between knight and queen. Try and key each do two things at once: 1.Be6 vacates c8 for Sc8 and closes the queen's 6th rank (no Qh6); 1.Ke4 vacates f5 for Sf5 and closes the queen's e-file (no Qxe5). In the set position both queen mates work after c5 (dual) and each phase kills one of them. His words: 'at first I just had two mates, then I somehow had to separate, that's obviously the hard part. Here it's square vacations and line changes for the queen. Not so simple geometrically.' Process (journal): 20 minutes on the d7/Ke6 setting found the pair of mates per step quickly; the selectors were bishop f6/d8 (knight mate) and king g5/f4 (queen mate), two different pieces, so no single move could switch both. He shifted the whole scheme one file left, after which one king move and one bishop move each carry both switches; he built the post-key position first (king on e4) and retracted the king to f5. The e5 pawn then refutes Be6 and cut the cooks from 11 keys to 4; wPd2 + bPd3 stop Qa3+, Qc3 and Qc1 (a search found no single unit that does it). Flaws: set play c6 and e4 unprovided, c5 set dual; the key takes the e4 move away from Black; zugzwang means the steps do not defend against anything; thin content (two variations, Black has two moves after the key); king key.

Explanation

Queen ambush behind the knight: 1.Qh5! (2.Qf7#). The knight's departure from f5 unmasks Qh3-e6 (so every knight move defends, Qe6 parries the threat) and opens h5-d5 for the random mate: S~ 2.Qd5#. Corrections close a second line on arrival: 1...Sd6 cuts both the rook's guard of d5 (so Qd5 fails) and the bishop's e7-c5 line, 2.Qxc5#; 1...Se3 cuts h3-d3, 2.Qe2#. The bishop on e7 leaves d6 as the only interference square, which is what removed the Sd6/Se7 twin dual of the earlier versions. The rook d8 is the point of the scheme and its price: 1...Sxd4 gave 2.Rxd4#/Qd5# until bPc5 (cxd4) was added with c5 covered by Ba3, which replaced two pawns (Pa3, Pb4). The queen plays key, threat and all three mates, from an active post to the ambush. No tries worth the name (1.Qb1?/1.Qa1? both fail to Sxd4!), no changed mates, no duals; every unit load-bearing. 15 units. His reservation: Sd6 carries a double effect and Se3 a single one; in a symmetrical theme the thematic variations should be roughly equal in effect, so the imbalance is a drawback.

bourd-bench-unpin-c3-bd3

gate pass3 tries · 0 changed

Bishop and knight unpin by interposing on c3; queen mates on both 6th-rank squares.

Key ['Bd3'] · E. Bourd (Composing Bench, 11 Oct 2026, session mv3ukaxu), from Claude's post-key sketch

2N5/3p1K1p/Q7/3nkB2/rbPn3N/6P1/1B6/8

Set
1...Sc3 2.Qf6#, 1...Bc3 2.Qd6#
Try
1.Bxh7? (2.Sf3#) 1...Sc3 2.Qf6#, 1...Bc3 2.Qd6#, but 1...Ra3!
Try
1.Bc2? (2.Sf3#) 1...Sc3 2.Qf6#, 1...Bc3 2.Qd6#, but 1...Ra3!
Try
1.Bb1? (2.Sf3#) 1...Sc3 2.Qf6#, 1...Bc3 2.Qd6#, but 1...Ra3!
Key
1.Bd3! (2.Sf3#) 1...Sc3 2.Qf6#, 1...Bc3 2.Qd6#
Explanation

1.Bd3! (2.Sf3#) Sc3 2.Qf6#, Bc3 2.Qd6#; tries 1.Bxh7?/Bc2?/Bb1? (same threat) Ra3!. Bb2 pins Sd4; both defences interpose on c3 and unpin it (Sxf3 possible). The bishop's departure from b4 gives up d6; the knight's from d5 gives up f6. The queen a6 mates on both along the 6th rank, so each sibling mate fails to the defender that stayed (Bxd6 / Sxf6). Key: the bishop leaves f5, where only Sh4 protected it (1.Sf3+? Kxf5), and from d3 it keeps e4/f5 and shields f3 from the black rook's 1...Ra3; the other retreats on b1-h7 fail to Ra3. His notes: he disliked 1...Bd6 also defending ('not clean'); he wanted the queen for both mates instead of an f2 pawn kept just for f4#; a third mate on e6 failed ('e6 is unpinned'). 'Can improve much more, but the scheme works.' Critique: same refutation Ra3 for three tries, static (both mates set), random knight moves allow Qf6 and Sf3; dual avoidance unified; 8+7.

bourd-two-bishops-sg6

gate pass1 tries · 0 changed

Two bishops cut the e-file far from the king, which opens Kxe5; try 1.Sh7? Be2!.

Key ['Sg6'] · E. Bourd (bench session mv4dvvuh, 11 Oct 2026), composed to show the process on his own theme

5N2/2KQ1p2/1ppp3n/1bbkBPp1/8/2R2P2/8/4R3

Set
1...Sg8/Sxf5/Sg4 2.Qxf7#, 1...Be3 2.Qxd6#
Try
1.Sh7? (2.Sf6#) 1...Sg8/Sg4 2.Qxf7#, 1...Be3 2.Qxd6#, but 1...Be2!
Key
1.Sg6! (2.Se7#) 1...Sg8/Sxf5 2.Qxf7#, 1...Be3 2.Qxd6#, 1...Be2 2.Qxc6#, 1...fxg6 2.Qe6#
Explanation

1.Sg6! (2.Se7#) Be2 2.Qxc6#, Be3 2.Qxd6#, fxg6 2.Qe6#, Sxf5/Sg8 2.Qxf7#; try 1.Sh7? (2.Sf6#) Be2! (Qxc6+ Kxe5: only the knight on g6 guards e5 after the cut). Re1 guards e5 (and e4 with Pf3); the threat Se7+ takes the knight's guard of e5 away, so the bishops defend by cutting the e-file on e2/e3, far from the king, which makes Kxe5 possible. Bb5 held c6, Bc5 held d6: Qxc6#/Qxd6#, and Qxd6 after Be2 or Qxc6 after Be3 is captured by the other bishop. Set play: Be3 Qxd6# set, Be2 unprovided (Kxe5 after Qxc6+), the key adds that mate. Every unit needed (trim); g5 stops the double threat Sf4#, Kc7 protects both mating queens. Gate PASS. Flaws: one try only (no try is refuted by Be3, since Qxd6 covers e5 itself); 7 pawns; Rc3 only guards c4; checking tries only otherwise. How he made it: scheme Kd5, Rh6, bishops c3/d3 cutting the 6th rank at f6/g6 (spread: line and cut squares away from the king); built the post-key with a knight threat; when the only key was the check 1.Rh4+ he moved the White king and queen, stripped Sa4, bQb1, bPb2, and turned the board a quarter (the black c2/c3/c4 chain that checked the king, captured on b3 and promoted became a static b6/c6/d6 chain, the targets of the mates); three changes later the post-key had no hole; findkey gave five unique keys (Sf8/Sh8/Sh4-g6, Rb3/Ra3-c3); he chose Sf8-g6 because f8 also gives the try Sh7?.

bourd-three-captures-e4

gate fail0 tries · 0 changed

Three black units capture the sacrificed key bishop on e4; each departure frees one knight mate, the others still guard. Unified dual avoidance. One phase, no tries: the closest to your exception (a sacrifice taken three ways, each capture freeing one knight mate), but your call.

Key ['Be4'] · Evgeni Bourd

1K6/1B6/8/p1N2Qnp/1b1k4/3P1bN1/1PPn1P2/7q

Key
1.Be4! (2.Qd5#) 1...Sgxe4 2.Se6#, 1...Bxe4 2.Se2#, 1...Sdxe4 2.Sb3#
Explanation

1.Be4! (2.Qd5#) Sgxe4 2.Se6#, Bxe4 2.Se2#, Sdxe4 2.Sb3#. The key piece is the one captured and it supplies the threat (Be4 guards d5), so every capture defends for the same reason; each capture's departure unguards one white knight's mating square (g5 left e6, f3 left e2, d2 left b3), and each sibling mate fails because the other capturers still guard their squares (unified dual avoidance). All captures self-block e4, but no mate relies on it. His order: threat -> pieces that can capture -> arrange mates -> find the key ('most of the part is just finding the key'). Not needed: bPa5 (16-unit version 1K6/1B6/8/2N2Qnp/1b1k4/3P1bN1/1PPn1P2/7q). Flaws: passive wK, bQh1 and bBb4 exist to refute tries (Bxf3, Qxg5, Sce4) and cooks, set duals after Sge4/Sde4/Bxc5 (unimportant), sacrificial-key-onto-the-square is the theme's classic form (Strebkovs 2003, his own Problemesis 2003 with Se6).
